en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Cūḷavagga 19.
The Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha (Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhaka)
1. The Request for the Recitation of the Pātimokkha.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Now on that occasion, on the Uposatha day, the Blessed One was seated surrounded by the community of monks.

Then, when the night was far spent and the first watch had passed, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
“The night, Bhante, is far spent; the first watch has passed; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time.
May the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus.”
When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.

A second time, as the night was far advanced and the middle watch had passed, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed him thus:
“The night, Bhante, is far advanced; the middle watch has passed; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time.”
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus.
A second time the Blessed One remained silent.
And a third time, when the night had advanced and the last watch had passed, the Venerable Ānanda rose.

When the night had turned crimson and the dawn was breaking, he rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he said to the Blessed One:
“The night has passed, Bhante; the final watch has ended, the dawn has risen, and the night is at its joyful conclusion. The community of monks has been sitting for a long time.”
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus.
"The assembly is not pure, Ānanda.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“With reference to what person, Ānanda, did the Blessed One say:
‘The assembly, Ānanda, is not pure’?
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna encompassed the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus with his mind and reflected upon it.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw that person— immoral, of evil nature, impure and of suspicious conduct,
secretive in his actions, a non-recluse claiming to be a recluse, not living the holy life while claiming to live the holy life,
internally rotten, leaking, and putrid— seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having seen him, he approached that person and, having approached, said this to him:
"Arise, friend! You have been seen by the Blessed One;
you no longer have communion with the bhikkhus."
When this was said, that person remained silent.
A second time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to that person:
"Arise, friend! You have been seen by the Blessed One."
"There is no association for you with the bhikkhus.
A second time, that person remained silent.
A third time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to that person:
“Get up, friend! You have been seen by the Blessed One;
you no longer have communion with the bhikkhus.
A third time, that person remained silent.

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna took that person by the arm, led him out through the outer gatehouse, and having given him the needle-and-pin [of the assembly], he approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"That person, Bhante, has been expelled by me;
the assembly is now pure."
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha for the bhikkhus.
“It is wonderful, Moggallāna! It is marvelous, Moggallāna! That foolish man will wait even until he is seized by the arm!
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
2. The Eight Marvels of the Great Ocean:
“Bhikkhus, there are these eight marvelous and wonderful qualities of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
What are the eight?
“Monks, the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and slants gradually, not falling off abruptly.
That the great ocean, monks, slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and slants gradually, not falling off abruptly— this, monks,
is the first wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.”
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean is stable and does not overstep its shore.
That the great ocean is stable and does not overstep its shore— this, monks,
is the second wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean does not dwell with a dead corpse. Whatever dead corpse there is in the great ocean, it quickly carries to the shore and casts up onto the dry land.

That, monks, the great ocean does not dwell with a dead corpse—that whatever dead corpse there is in the great ocean, it quickly carries to the shore and casts up onto the dry land—is the third wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, monks, whatever great rivers there are— namely, the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī,
the Sarabhū, and the Mahī— when they reach the great ocean, they abandon their former names and lineages and are reckoned simply as the "great ocean.

That, monks, is how whatever great rivers there are— the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī— when they reach the great ocean, abandon their former names and lineages and are reckoned simply as the "great ocean."
This, monks, is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, monks, whatever rivers in the world flow into the great ocean, and whatever showers fall from the sky, the great ocean shows neither depletion nor fullness because of them.
Furthermore, monks, whatever rivers flow into the great ocean from the world, and whatever torrents fall from the sky, the great ocean shows neither decrease nor increase because of them.
This, monks, is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean has a single taste: the taste of salt.

Furthermore, monks, the great ocean has a single taste, the taste of salt—this, monks, is the sixth astounding and amazing quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Moreover, monks, the great ocean possesses many jewels, numerous jewels. These are the jewels therein:
That is to say: pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, gold, rubies, and cat’s-eye gems.

And because, monks, the great ocean possesses many treasures and manifold treasures, and these are the treasures therein—that is to say, pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, gold, rubies, and cat’s-eye gems—this, monks, is the seventh astounding and amazing quality of the great ocean, seeing which again and again the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, monks, the great ocean is the abode of great beings. Therein are these beings:
the *timi*, the *timiṅgala*, the *timitimiṅgala*, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas.

In the great ocean there are individual bodies a hundred yojanas long, individual bodies two hundred yojanas long, individual bodies three hundred yojanas long, and individual bodies four hundred yojanas long.
There are bodies, monks, even five hundred yojanas in length.
Furthermore, monks, that the great ocean is the abode of great beings—therein are these beings:
the *timi*, the *timiṅgala*, the *timitimiṅgala*, the *asuras*, the *nāgas*, and the *gandhabbas*; there are in the great ocean bodies even five hundred yojanas in length.
…pe… there are even bodies five hundred yojanas long— this, monks,
is the eighth astounding and amazing quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
These, monks, are the eight astounding and amazing qualities of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.”
3. Eight Marvels in This Dhamma and Vinaya.
“In the same way, monks, there are eight marvelous and wonderful qualities in this Dhamma and Vinaya, which the monks, having seen them again and again, take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
What are the eight?”
Just as, monks, the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and shelves gradually, not plunging all at once into a steep depth;
even so, monks, in this Dhamma and Discipline there is gradual training, gradual performance, and gradual practice, and there is no penetration to final knowledge all at once.
That, monks, which is the gradual training, gradual performance, and gradual practice in this Dhamma and Discipline, and the lack of penetration to final knowledge all at once—this is it.
This, monks, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which monks take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline. Just as, monks,
the great ocean is stable in nature and does not overstep its shore,
even so, monks, whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, that my disciples do not transgress even for the sake of their lives.

Moreover, monks, that training rule which has been laid down by me for my disciples, even for the sake of their lives, my disciples do not transgress it—this, monks, is the second wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya, seeing which, seeing which, the monks delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Just as, monks, the great ocean does not dwell with a dead corpse; whatever dead corpse there is in the great ocean, it quickly carries it to the shore and casts it up onto the dry land.
In the same way, monks, that person who is immoral, of evil nature, of impure and suspicious conduct, secretive in his actions,
one who is not a recluse yet claims to be a recluse, one who does not live the holy life yet claims to live the holy life,
who is internally rotten, leaking, and full of filth— the Saṅgha does not dwell together with him; rather, having assembled quickly, they suspend him.
Even though such a person may be sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he is nonetheless far from the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha is far from him.
For, bhikkhus, that person who is immoral, of evil nature, impure and of suspicious conduct, secretive in his actions, not a recluse yet claiming to be a recluse,
not living the holy life yet claiming to live the holy life— internally rotten, leaking, and putrid like a drain-pipe— is indeed far from the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha does not dwell together with him; having assembled quickly, it suspends him.
Even though he may be sitting in the midst of the community of monks, he is nonetheless far removed from the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha is far removed from him.
Monks, this is the third wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya, seeing which monks take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
“Just as, monks, whatever great rivers there are— namely, the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī,
the Sarabhū, and the Mahī— when they reach the great ocean, they abandon their former names and lineages and are reckoned simply as ‘the great ocean’;
even so, monks, these four castes— the khattiyas, the brāhmaṇas, the vessas, and the suddas— [when they enter the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata...]”

Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness in this Dhamma and Vinaya, they abandon their former names and clans and come to be reckoned simply as "ascetics, sons of the Sakyan. And furthermore, monks,
these four castes— the khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, and suddas— when they have entered upon the path proclaimed by the Tathāgata...

Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness in this Dhamma and Vinaya, they abandon their former names and clans and come to be reckoned simply as "ascetics, sons of the Sakyan"— this, monks,
is the fourth astounding and amazing quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya, which the monks, seeing again and again, take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
“Just as, monks, whatever rivers in the world flow into the great ocean and whatever showers of rain fall from the sky, the great ocean is not seen to be diminished or filled by that;
even so, monks, though many bhikkhus attain final nibbāna through the element of nibbāna without residue, the element of nibbāna is not seen to be diminished or filled by that.”
“Furthermore, monks, even if many bhikkhus attain final nibbāna by the element of nibbāna without residue, neither a deficiency nor a fullness is perceived in that element of nibbāna.
This, monks, is the fifth astounding and amazing quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which the bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Just as, monks, the great ocean has a single taste, the taste of salt;”
In the same way, monks, this Dhamma and Vinaya has a single flavor: the flavor of liberation.

That this Dhamma and Vinaya has a single flavor—the flavor of liberation—is, monks, the sixth marvelous and wonderful quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya, seeing which, seeing which, the monks take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya.

"Monks, just as the great ocean is rich in treasures, possessing many treasures, and therein are these treasures, namely: pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, gold, rubies, and masāragalla stones;
even so, monks, this Dhamma and Discipline is rich in treasures, possessing many treasures. And therein are these treasures, namely:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, and the five faculties."
The five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.

Furthermore, monks, this Dhamma and Discipline possesses many jewels, manifold jewels; therein these are the jewels, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness ... [and so on] ... the noble eightfold path.
This, monks, is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which, seeing which, the monks take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Just as, monks, the great ocean is the abode of great beings—therein are these beings:
the *timi*, the *timiṅgala*, the *timitimiṅgala*, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas;
there are in the great ocean individual bodies a hundred leagues long, two hundred leagues long, three hundred leagues long, and even four hundred leagues long.
There are even selfhoods five hundred yojanas in size;
in the very same way, monks, this Dhamma and Discipline is the abode of great beings. These are the beings:
the stream-enterer, and one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the once-returner, and one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning.
One who has entered the path; one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; an arahant; and one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship.

And because, monks, this Dhamma and Discipline is the abode of great beings, these are the beings therein: the stream-enterer, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry … [and so on] … the arahant, and one practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship.
“Monks, this is the eighth astounding and wonderful quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, which the monks see again and again and take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
These, monks, are the eight astounding and wonderful qualities in this Dhamma and Discipline, which the monks see again and again and take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the significance of this, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation (udāna):
“The rain pours down upon that which is covered,
but it does not pour down upon that which is open;
therefore, uncover what is covered.”
“Thus the rain will not drench him.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: [4. Worthy of Hearing the Pātimokkha]...
“Monks, from this day forward, I shall no longer perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha.
Monks, from this day forward, you yourselves should perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha.
It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen that the Tathāgata would perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha with an assembly that is not pure.”
"Monks, one who has committed an offense should not listen to the Pātimokkha.
Whoever should listen, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I authorize that the Pātimokkha be suspended for whoever listens to the Pātimokkha while having an offense."
And furthermore, monks, it should be set aside in this way:
on the Uposatha day of the fourteenth or the fifteenth, when that person is present, it should be announced in the midst of the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.”
“A person named so-and-so is guilty of an offense; I suspend the Pātimokkha for him; the Pātimokkha should not be recited in his presence.
In this way, the Pātimokkha is suspended. Now at that time, the group of six monks, thinking, “Let no one know of us,” listened to the Pātimokkha while they were still guilty of offenses.
The elder bhikkhus, who were knowers of others' minds, informed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, such-and-such and such-and-such of the group-of-six bhikkhus,
thinking 'no one knows us,' listen to the Pātimokkha while still possessing offenses."
The group-of-six monks heard:
“It seems that the elder monks, who are knowers of others’ minds, are informing us monks:
‘Friends, such-and-such and such-and-such group-of-six monks—’”
“‘No one knows us,’ they thought, and so they listened to the Pātimokkha while still guilty of offenses.
Then [the monks] said, “Previously, our well-behaved monks used to suspend the recitation of the Pātimokkha.”
They suspend the Pātimokkha for pure monks who have committed no offense, when there is no basis and no reason.
Those monks who are of few desires... [as above] ...were indignant, disparaged, and complained, saying:
"How can these monks of the group of six suspend the Pātimokkha for pure monks who have committed no offense, when there is no basis and no reason?"
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ...
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that the group-of-six bhikkhus cancel the Pātimokkha for pure bhikkhus who have committed no offense, without ground and without cause?
“It is true, Blessed One.”... [as before] ...
Having rebuked them...
and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
"Monks, the Pātimokkha must not be suspended for pure monks who are without offense, without basis, and without cause."
Whoever should set it aside, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
5. The Setting Aside of the Pātimokkha, Lawful and Unlawful:
Monks, there is one way of setting aside the Pātimokkha that is unlawful, and one way that is lawful.
There are two ways of suspending the Pātimokkha that are illegitimate and two that are legitimate;
three ways of suspending the Pātimokkha that are illegitimate and three that are legitimate;
four ways of suspending the Pātimokkha that are illegitimate and four that are legitimate.
There are five unrighteous ways of suspending the Pātimokkha and five righteous ways;
six unrighteous ways of suspending the Pātimokkha and six righteous ways;
seven unrighteous ways of suspending the Pātimokkha and seven righteous ways.
There are eight unrighteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha and eight righteous ones;
nine unrighteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha and nine righteous ones;
ten unrighteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha and ten righteous ones.
What is the one kind of suspension of the Pātimokkha that is contrary to the Dhamma?
One suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in virtue—
this is the one kind of suspension of the Pātimokkha that is contrary to the Dhamma.
What is the one legitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha?
One suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a failure in virtue that has a root;
this is the one legitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha.
What are the two unrighteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha?

One suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in morality; one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in conduct—these are the two unrighteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the two lawful suspensions of the Pātimokkha?

One suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a failure in morality accompanied by its root; one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a failure in conduct accompanied by its root—these are the two lawful suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the three unrighteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha?

One suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in morality; one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in conduct; one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in view.
These are the three unrighteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the three legitimate suspensions of the Pātimokkha?

One suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a failure in virtue accompanied by its root; one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a failure in conduct accompanied by its root; one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a failure in view accompanied by its root.
These are the three legitimate suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the four unrighteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha?
One suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in morality; one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in conduct;
one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in view; one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in livelihood.
He suspends the Pātimokkha—
these are the four unrighteous ways of suspending the Pātimokkha.
What are the four righteous ways of suspending the Pātimokkha?
He suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a failure in virtue that has a basis; he suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a failure in conduct that has a basis;
he suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a failure in view that has a basis; he suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a failure in livelihood that has a basis.
These are the four legitimate ways of suspending the Pātimokkha.
What are the five illegitimate ways of suspending the Pātimokkha?

One suspends the Pātimokkha on the basis of a groundless charge of an offense entailing expulsion; one suspends it on the basis of a groundless charge of an offense entailing suspension... [and so forth].
If he suspends the Pātimokkha by means of a groundless offense entailing expiation (pācittiya),
or by means of a groundless offense entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya),
or by means of a groundless offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa): [this is an offense of wrong-doing].
These are the five unrighteous ways of suspending the Pātimokkha.
What are the five righteous ways of suspending the Pātimokkha?
One suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a *pārājika* offense together with its root; one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a *saṅghādisesa* offense together with its root... [and so forth].

If one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of an offense entailing confession (pācittiya), or on account of an offense entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya), or on account of an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)—
These are the five lawful suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the six unlawful suspensions of the Pātimokkha?

One suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in morality that has not been committed; one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in morality that has been committed.
He suspends the Pātimokkha for groundless failure in conduct when it has not been committed; he suspends the Pātimokkha for groundless failure in conduct when it has been committed;

he suspends the Pātimokkha for groundless failure in view when it has not been committed; he suspends the Pātimokkha for groundless failure in view when it has been committed—these are the six unlawful suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the six legitimate suspensions of the Pātimokkha?

He suspends the Pātimokkha when there has been a failure in morality accompanied by its root, though it has not yet been committed; he suspends the Pātimokkha when there has been a failure in morality accompanied by its root, once it has been committed; [he suspends the Pātimokkha] when there has been a failure in conduct accompanied by its root... [and so on].
He suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a failure in view when none has occurred … [and] when one has occurred—
these are the six lawful suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the seven unrighteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha?
One suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense; one suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless charge of a *saṅghādisesa* offense...
[and so on] ...of a *thullaccaya*, a *pācittiya*, a *pāṭidesanīya*, a *dukkaṭa*, or a *dubbhāsita* offense.
These are the seven unrighteous ways of suspending the Pātimokkha.
What are the seven righteous ways of suspending the Pātimokkha?
One suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a *pārājika* offense together with its root; one suspends it on account of a *saṅghādisesa* offense together with its root... [and so forth].
One suspends the Pātimokkha for a thullaccaya offense, a pācittiya offense, a pāṭidesanīya offense, a dukkaṭa offense, or a dubbhāsita offense—
these are the seven legitimate suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the eight illegitimate suspensions of the Pātimokkha?

He suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in virtue when no such failure has occurred; he suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in virtue when such a failure has occurred;
[he does so] on account of a groundless failure in conduct …pe… on account of a groundless failure in view …pe…
He suspends the Pātimokkha because of a failure in livelihood when none has occurred … [and so on] … when one has occurred—
these are the eight illegitimate suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the eight legitimate suspensions of the Pātimokkha?

He suspends the Pātimokkha for a breach of morality with a basis, even when that breach of morality has not been committed; he suspends the Pātimokkha for a breach of morality with a basis, even when that breach of morality has been committed.
[Likewise] for a breach of conduct with a basis … for a breach of view with a basis … [and so on].
He suspends the Pātimokkha when there has been no failure of livelihood, yet he does so when there has been one—
these are the eight lawful suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the nine unlawful suspensions of the Pātimokkha?

He suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in virtue that has not been committed; he suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in virtue that has been committed; he suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in virtue that has both been committed and not committed.

He suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in conduct … [and so on] … he suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in view that has not been committed … [and so on] … he suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in view that has been committed … [and so on].
Regarding what has been done and what has not been done— these are the nine unrighteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the nine righteous suspensions of the Pātimokkha?

He suspends the Pātimokkha for a breach of morality accompanied by its root when it has not been committed; he suspends the Pātimokkha for a breach of morality accompanied by its root when it has been committed; he suspends the Pātimokkha for a breach of morality accompanied by its root when it has both been committed and not committed.

[The same applies to] a breach of conduct accompanied by its root … down to … he suspends the Pātimokkha for a breach of view accompanied by its root when it has not been committed … down to … when it has been committed … down to … [when it has both been committed and not committed].
Regarding what has been done and what has not been done— these are the nine lawful suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
What are the ten unlawful suspensions of the Pātimokkha?
One who has committed a *pārājika* offense is not sitting in that assembly, nor is the discussion regarding a *pārājika* offense unfinished;
one who has renounced the training is not sitting in that assembly, nor is the discussion regarding the renunciation of the training unfinished;
he enters into a legitimate concord, he does not reject a legitimate concord, and the discussion regarding the rejection of a legitimate concord is not unfinished.

One is not suspected of having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense] regarding failure in virtue; one is not suspected of having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense] regarding failure in conduct; one is not suspected of having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense] regarding failure in view—these are the ten unrighteous ways of suspending the Pātimokkha.
What are the ten righteous ways of suspending the Pātimokkha?
A person who has committed a pārājika offense is sitting in that assembly, and the discussion regarding the pārājika offense is unfinished;
a person who has renounced the training is sitting in that assembly, and the discussion regarding the renunciation of the training is unfinished;
they do not attain a legitimate concord, they reject a legitimate concord, and the discussion regarding the rejection of a legitimate concord is unfinished.

One is suspected of having been seen, heard, or expected [to have committed] a failure in virtue; one is suspected of having been seen, heard, or expected [to have committed] a failure in conduct; one is suspected of having been seen, heard, or expected [to have committed] a failure in view.
These are the ten legitimate suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
6. Legitimate Suspension of the Pātimokkha.
How is it that one who is defeated sits in that assembly?
Here, monks, by whatever modes, whatever characteristics, and whatever signs there is an offense against a rule involving defeat,
by those modes, those characteristics, and those signs, a monk sees another monk as one who has committed a defeat.
While a monk is committing an offense entailing defeat, another monk does not see him committing that offense; however, another monk informs the first monk, saying:
“Friend, the monk so-and-so has committed an offense entailing defeat.”
It may be that a bhikkhu does not see another bhikkhu committing an offense entailing expulsion, nor does another bhikkhu inform him, saying:
“Friend, such-and-such a bhikkhu has committed an offense entailing expulsion”; rather, that bhikkhu himself informs the other bhikkhu, saying:
“Friend, I have committed an offense entailing expulsion.”

“Monks, if a monk so desires, on the Uposatha day—the fourteenth or the fifteenth—on account of what he has seen, heard, or suspected, he may, in the midst of the Saṅgha and in the presence of that person, declare:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This person named so-and-so has committed an offense involving defeat; I suspend the Pātimokkha for him; the Pātimokkha is not to be recited in his presence.’”
This is the legitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha.
When the Pātimokkha has been suspended for a bhikkhu, the assembly disperses due to one of ten obstacles:
an obstacle from a king, an obstacle from thieves, an obstacle from fire, an obstacle from water, or an obstacle from humans.
Or by an obstacle caused by non-human beings, or an obstacle caused by wild animals, or an obstacle caused by reptiles,
or an obstacle to life, or an obstacle to the holy life.
Should a bhikkhu so desire, monks, he may declare it in that very residence or in another residence, in the presence of that person or in the midst of the Saṅgha:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
A discussion concerning an offense entailing expulsion has been interrupted regarding a certain person; that matter remains undecided.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha decide that matter.’
If this can be obtained, that is good.
If it cannot be obtained, then on the Uposatha day, whether on the fourteenth or the fifteenth, when that person is present, one should declare it in the midst of the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me."
"The discussion regarding an offense entailing expulsion for a person named so-and-so is unfinished; that matter has not yet been adjudicated.
Therefore, I suspend the Pātimokkha for him; the Pātimokkha should not be recited in his presence.
This is the legitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha.
How does one who has renounced the training sit in that assembly?
Here, monks, by whatever modes, whatever characteristics, and whatever signs the renunciation of the training occurs, by those same modes,
those characteristics, and those signs, a monk sees another monk who has renounced the training.
Not only does a monk see another monk who has renounced the training, but also another monk informs him:
“Friend, a monk named so-and-so has renounced the training.
Not only does a monk see another monk who has renounced the training, nor does another monk inform him [of it]...
‘Friend, the training has been renounced by the monk named so-and-so,’ yet that very monk informs another monk:
‘Friend, the training has been renounced by me.

Desiring [to act], monks, on the basis of what was seen, heard, or suspected, a monk may, on the Uposatha day—the fourteenth or the fifteenth—when that person is present, declare it in the midst of the Saṅgha:
‘Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
A person named so-and-so has renounced the training; I suspend the Pātimokkha for him, and the Pātimokkha should not be recited in his presence.
This is a legitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha.
When the Pātimokkha has been suspended for a bhikkhu, and the assembly has departed due to one of the ten obstacles—
whether an obstacle from a king,

or [as the case may be] an obstacle to the holy life— a bhikkhu who so desires, monks, may, in that same residence or in another residence, when that person is present, declare it in the midst of the Saṅgha:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
The discussion regarding the person named so-and-so who has renounced the training is unfinished; that matter has not yet been adjudicated.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha adjudicate that matter.’
If this can be obtained in this way, that is good.
If it cannot be obtained, then on the Uposatha day—the fourteenth or the fifteenth—when that person is present, one should declare it in the midst of the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me."
“The discussion regarding the renunciation of training by the person named so-and-so is unfinished; that matter has not been adjudicated.
Therefore, I suspend the Pātimokkha for him; the Pātimokkha should not be recited while he is present.
This is a legitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha.
How does one fail to attain a legitimate concord?
Here, monks, by whatever modes, whatever characteristics, and whatever signs there is the failure to attain a legitimate concord,
by those very modes, those very characteristics, and those very signs, a monk [disregards] a monk.
He sees a monk who is not entering into lawful concord.
Furthermore, it may be that a monk does not see another monk who is not entering into lawful concord, but rather another monk informs him:
"Friend, such-and-such a monk is not entering into lawful concord."
It may be that a bhikkhu does not see another bhikkhu failing to attend to a legitimate communal harmony, nor does another bhikkhu inform him, saying, “Friend,
such-and-such a bhikkhu is not attending to a legitimate communal harmony”; rather, that bhikkhu himself informs the other bhikkhu,
saying, “Friend, I am not attending to a legitimate communal harmony.”

“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu so desires, on the Uposatha day—the fourteenth or the fifteenth—on account of what he has seen, heard, or suspected, he should, in the midst of the Saṅgha and in the presence of that person, declare:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This person named so-and-so does not attend to lawful concord; I suspend the Pātimokkha for him; the Pātimokkha is not to be recited in his presence.’”
‘the lawful suspension of the Pātimokkha.
How does one reject a lawful concord?
Here, monks, a monk [rejects] a lawful concord by means of those modes, those signs, and those characteristics...
There is a subsequent refusal: by those modes, those characteristics, and those signs, a monk sees another monk refusing a legitimate unity.
Or, even though a monk does not see another monk refusing a legitimate unity, another monk informs him: "Friend, the monk named so-and-so is refusing a legitimate unity."
It is not only that a bhikkhu sees another bhikkhu rejecting a legitimate unity, nor that another bhikkhu informs him,
saying, ‘Friend, such-and-such a bhikkhu is rejecting a legitimate unity,’ but rather that the bhikkhu himself informs the other bhikkhu, saying, ‘Friend, I am rejecting a legitimate unity.’

“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu so desires, on the Uposatha day—the fourteenth or the fifteenth—on account of what he has seen, heard, or suspected, when that person is present in the midst of the Saṅgha, he should declare:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This person named so-and-so rejects lawful concord. I suspend the Pātimokkha for him; the Pātimokkha should not be recited in his presence.’”
This is the legitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha.
When the Pātimokkha has been suspended for a bhikkhu, the assembly disperses due to one of ten obstacles—
such as a royal obstacle, and so forth.
Or by an obstacle to the holy life.
Should a bhikkhu so desire, monks, he may declare it either in that very residence or in another residence, in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the presence of that person:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me."
“The discussion regarding the granting of formal unity for the person named so-and-so has been interrupted; that matter remains undecided.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha decide upon that matter.
If this can be obtained, it is good.
If he does not obtain it, then on the Uposatha day, whether on the fourteenth or the fifteenth, when that person is present in the midst of the Saṅgha, it should be declared:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
The discussion regarding the withdrawal of formal consent from the person named so-and-so for his lawful reconciliation has been interrupted; that matter remains undecided."
"I suspend the Pātimokkha for him; the Pātimokkha should not be recited in his presence"—this is the legitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha.
How is one seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in virtue?
Furthermore, monks, in this case, by whatever modes, whatever characteristics, and whatever signs a monk is seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in virtue,
by those same modes, those same characteristics, and those same signs, he sees another monk who is seen, heard,
or suspected of a failure in virtue.
Not only does a bhikkhu see another bhikkhu suspected of a failure in virtue on account of what has been seen, heard, or suspected; rather, another bhikkhu informs him:
“Friend, such-and-such a bhikkhu is suspected of a failure in virtue on account of what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
Not only does a bhikkhu see another bhikkhu suspected of a failure in virtue on account of what has been seen, heard, or suspected, nor does another bhikkhu inform him; [but...]
‘Friends, such-and-such a monk has been seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in virtue. Furthermore, that very monk informs another monk:
‘Friends, I have been seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in virtue.

Monks, if he so desires, on the Uposatha day—the fourteenth or the fifteenth—he should, in the midst of the Saṅgha and in the presence of that person, declare it based on what was seen, heard, or suspected:
‘Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
The person named so-and-so has been seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in virtue; I suspend the Pātimokkha for him, and the Pātimokkha should not be recited while he is present.
This is a legitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha.
How is it that one is seen, heard, or suspected of failure in conduct?
Here, monks, a monk— by whatever modes, whatever signs, and whatever characteristics one is seen, heard, or suspected of failure in conduct—
is [regarded] by those same modes, those same signs, and those same characteristics as a monk...
He sees a monk who has been seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in conduct.
Or rather, a monk does not see another monk who has been seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in conduct; instead, another monk informs him:
“Friend, such-and-such a monk has been seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in conduct.”
It may be that a bhikkhu does not see another bhikkhu as having fallen away from proper conduct, nor has he heard of it, nor suspects it;

nor does another bhikkhu inform him, saying, "Friend, such-and-such a bhikkhu is seen, heard, or suspected to have fallen away from proper conduct. Rather, that bhikkhu himself informs the other bhikkhu, saying, "Friend, I am seen, heard, or suspected to have fallen away from proper conduct."

“Monks, if a monk so desires, on the observance day—the fourteenth or the fifteenth—having seen that [offense], having heard that, or having suspected it, he may, in the midst of the Saṅgha and in the presence of that person, declare:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This person named so-and-so has been seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in conduct. I suspend the Pātimokkha for him; the Pātimokkha is not to be recited in his presence.’”
‘the lawful suspension of the Pātimokkha.
How does one become seen, heard, or suspected of failure in view?
Here, monks, a monk, by whatever modes, signs, or characteristics, [is known] to have failed in view...

He is suspected on account of what has been seen or heard; by those modes, those characteristics, and those signs, a monk sees another monk as being suspected on account of what has been seen or heard regarding a failure in view.
Or, it may be that a monk does not see another monk as being suspected on account of what has been seen or heard regarding a failure in view, but rather another monk informs him [of this].
‘Friend, such-and-such a bhikkhu has been seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in view.

Yet that bhikkhu does not see another bhikkhu who has been seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in view, nor does another bhikkhu inform him, saying, ‘Friend, such-and-such a bhikkhu has been seen, heard, or suspected of a failure in view’; rather, it is that very bhikkhu himself who informs the other bhikkhu.
‘Friend, I am seen, heard, or suspected by you to have failed in view.

If he so desires, monks, that bhikkhu—on account of what was seen, heard, or suspected—should, on the Uposatha day, whether on the fourteenth or the fifteenth, when that person is present, declare it in the midst of the Saṅgha:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
“A person named so-and-so is suspected of failure in view on account of what has been seen or heard; I suspend the Pātimokkha for him; the Pātimokkha is not to be recited in his presence.
This is the legitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha.
These are the ten legitimate suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
The first recitation section is finished.
7. The Factors of Formal Acceptance (Attādāna-aṅga).
Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, by a bhikkhu who wishes to take formal possession (*attādāna*), what kind of formal possession should be taken?
“Upāli, by a bhikkhu who wishes to take formal possession, a formal possession endowed with five factors should be taken.”
Upāli, a bhikkhu who wishes to take up the adoption of a self (*attādāna*) should reflect thus:
“As for this adoption of a self that I wish to take up, is now the time to take it up, or is it not?
If, Upāli, while reflecting, the bhikkhu knows thus:
‘This is not the right time to take this formal act upon oneself; it is not the right time,’ then, Upāli, that formal act should not be taken.
But if, Upāli, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows:
‘This is the right time to take this formal act upon oneself; it is not the wrong time,’ then, Upāli, that bhikkhu should reflect further:
‘This self-assertion that I wish to take up—is it indeed real, or is it not?
Upāli, if a bhikkhu, upon reflection, knows thus:
‘This self-assertion is unreal, it is not real,’ then, Upāli, that self-assertion should not be taken up.
But if, Upāli, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
"This taking up of self is real, not unreal," then, Upāli, that bhikkhu should reflect further:
"Is this taking up of self that I desire to take up conducive to welfare, or is it not?"
If, Upāli, a bhikkhu, upon reviewing, knows thus:
"This undertaking is conducive to harm, not conducive to benefit," then, Upāli, that undertaking should not be undertaken.
But if, Upāli, a bhikkhu, upon reviewing, knows thus: [it is conducive to benefit]...
‘This acquisition is connected with benefit, not unconnected with benefit,’ then, Upāli, that bhikkhu should further reflect:
‘When I take this acquisition, will I gain the support of the bhikkhus who are seen and trusted, according to the Dhamma and the Vinaya, or not?
If, Upāli, while reflecting, the bhikkhu knows thus:

“Upāli, if a monk, while taking up this formal act of self-accusation (*attādāna*), thinks: ‘By taking up this self-accusation, I will not obtain support from my friends and companions among the monks in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya,’ then that self-accusation should not be taken up.
But if, Upāli, while reflecting, a monk knows:
‘By taking up this self-accusation, I will obtain support from my friends and companions among the monks in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya,’ then, Upāli, that monk should reflect further:”

‘As I take up this personal initiative, will it lead to quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute within the Saṅgha, to a schism in the Saṅgha, a fracture in the Saṅgha, a division in the Saṅgha, and a separation in the Saṅgha—or will it not?
If, Upāli, upon reflection, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘As I take up this personal initiative, it will lead to quarreling, strife, and contention within the Saṅgha…’ [and so forth].
‘conflict, dispute, schism in the Saṅgha, fracture in the Saṅgha, formal separation of the Saṅgha,
and division of the Saṅgha,’ then, Upāli, that claim should not be taken up by him.
But if, Upāli, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
“Upāli, if one thinks, ‘By taking this formal act upon myself, there will be no quarrel, dispute, contention, or conflict for the Saṅgha arising from that cause;
no schism in the Saṅgha, no fracture in the Saṅgha, no division of the Saṅgha, and no separation within the Saṅgha,’ then that formal act should be taken.”
“Upāli, when a formal accusation (*attādāna*) is undertaken that is endowed with these five factors, it will not give rise to remorse later.
8. Factors to be Examined by the Accuser “Venerable sir, how many qualities should a monk who wishes to accuse another examine within himself before he accuses that other?”
“Upāli, a monk who wishes to reprove another should first examine himself with regard to five things before reproving the other.
Upāli, a monk wishing to reprove another should reflect thus:
‘Am I pure in my bodily conduct? Am I endowed with pure bodily conduct that is unbroken and flawless? Does this quality exist in me, or does it not?’”
“Furthermore, Upāli, if a bhikkhu is not pure in his bodily conduct, though he is possessed of pure bodily conduct that is unbroken and flawless, there will be those who say of him:
‘Come now, let the venerable one train in bodily conduct. Such will be the reproachers of him.
Again, Upāli, a bhikkhu who wishes to reprove another should reflect thus:”
‘Am I indeed one whose verbal conduct is pure; am I endowed with pure verbal conduct that is unbroken and flawless?
If, Upāli, a monk is not one whose verbal conduct is pure, nor endowed with pure verbal conduct that is unbroken and flawless, there will be those who say of him: [“...”]
‘Come now, let the venerable one train first in verbal conduct.
Such will be the reprovers of him. Furthermore, Upāli, a monk who wishes to reprove another must reflect thus:
‘Is my mind established in loving-kindness toward my fellow practitioners of the holy life, free from resentment? Does this quality exist in me, or does it not?’
In this case, Upāli, if a bhikkhu has not established a mind of loving-kindness toward his fellow practitioners in a state free from resentment, there will be those who say to him:
“Come now, Venerable One, please establish a mind of loving-kindness toward your fellow practitioners.
Such, Upāli, are those who would speak to him. Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu who wishes to reprove another should reflect in this way:
‘Am I indeed one who has heard much, who retains what he has heard, and who accumulates what he has heard? Are those teachings— which are beautiful in the beginning,
beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end, which proclaim in spirit and in letter the holy life that is entirely complete and pure—
such teachings as these that have been heard much by me, mastered, committed to memory, and examined with the mind?’
"Has this been well-penetrated by view? Does this Dhamma exist within me, or does it not?

If, Upāli, a bhikkhu is not learned, does not retain what he has heard, and does not accumulate what he has heard—those teachings which are beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end, in spirit and in letter, absolutely complete and pure—[he will not have well-penetrated them by view]."

They praise the holy life, yet such teachings as these are not much heard by him, nor are they retained, mastered by word, examined by mind, or well-penetrated by view. There will be those who say of him:
“Come now, let the venerable one first master the tradition. Thus there will be those who speak to him.
Furthermore, Upāli, a monk who wishes to reprove another should reflect thus:

‘Are both Pātimokkhas well-mastered by me in detail, well-analyzed, well-recited, and well-determined, both in terms of the rules and their specific characteristics? Does this quality exist in me or not?
If, Upāli, both Pātimokkhas are not well-mastered by the monk in detail, well-analyzed, [and so forth...]

If one has not mastered the teachings that have been well-proclaimed, well-expounded by the Blessed One—those that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the letter—and if, when questioned about them "sutta by sutta" and "phrase by phrase," asking "But where, friends, was this spoken by the Blessed One? one cannot provide an answer, there will be those who say of him:
"Come now, let the venerable one master the Vinaya. Thus there will be those who speak of him.
“Upāli, a monk who wishes to reprove another should first examine these five qualities within himself before reproving the other.
9. Qualities to be Established by the Reprover “Venerable sir, how many qualities should a monk who wishes to reprove another establish within himself before reproving the other?”
“Upāli, a bhikkhu who wishes to reprove another should first establish five qualities within himself before reproving the other:
‘I will speak at the proper time, not at an improper time;
I will speak what is true, not what is false.’”
"I shall speak gently, not harshly;
I shall speak what is beneficial, not what is unbeneficial;
I shall speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred."
“Upāli, a monk who wishes to reprove another should first establish these five qualities within himself before reproving the other.
10. Discourse on the One Who Reproves and the One Reproved “Venerable sir, in how many ways should remorse be induced in a monk who reproves contrary to the Dhamma?”
“Upāli, remorse should be induced in a monk who reproves unrighteously in five ways:
‘Venerable sir, you reproved at the wrong time, not at the right time; enough for you to feel remorse.
You reproved on the basis of what is untrue, not on the basis of what is true; enough for you to feel remorse.’”
"Venerable sir, you reproved me harshly, not gently; that is sufficient reason for you to feel remorse.
Venerable sir, you reproved me with what is unbeneficial, not with what is beneficial; that is sufficient reason for you to feel remorse.
Venerable sir, you reproved me while harboring hatred within, not with a mind of loving-kindness; that is sufficient reason for you to feel remorse."
“Upāli, remorse should be induced in a monk who reproves according to what is not the Dhamma by these five ways.
For what reason?
So that no other monk might think that one should be reproved with what is untrue.”
“But, Bhante, in how many ways should remorse be removed for a bhikkhu who has been reproved contrary to the Dhamma?
“Upāli, in five ways remorse should be removed for a bhikkhu who has been reproved contrary to the Dhamma:
‘Venerable sir, you were reproved at an improper time, not at the proper time; this is sufficient for you to be without remorse.’”
The venerable one has been reproved with what is untrue, not with what is true; that is sufficient for you to be without remorse.
The venerable one has been reproved harshly, not gently; that is sufficient for you to be without remorse.
The venerable one has been reproved with what is unbeneficial, not with what is beneficial; that is sufficient for you to be without remorse.
“Venerable sir, the venerable one was reproved with fault-finding, not with a mind of loving-kindness; that is sufficient for him to be free from remorse.
“Upāli, in these five ways, freedom from remorse should be established for a bhikkhu who has been reproved contrary to the Dhamma.
“Bhante, in how many ways should freedom from remorse be established for a bhikkhu who reproves according to the Dhamma?”
“Upāli, a monk who reproves according to the Dhamma should be inspired with freedom from remorse in five ways:
the venerable one reproves at the proper time, not at an improper time—this is sufficient for his freedom from remorse;
the venerable one reproves based on what is factual, not on what is unfactual—this is sufficient for his freedom from remorse.”
The venerable one reproves you gently, not harshly; this is sufficient for you to be free from remorse.
The venerable one reproves you with what is beneficial, not with what is unbeneficial; this is sufficient for you to be free from remorse.
The venerable one reproves you with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred; this is sufficient for you to be free from remorse.
“Upāli, in these five ways, freedom from remorse should be instilled in a monk who reproves according to the Dhamma.
For what reason?
So that another monk might also think: ‘One should reprove [others] based on what is factual.’”
“But, Bhante, in how many ways should remorse be induced in a bhikkhu who has been reproved in accordance with the Dhamma?
“Upāli, in five ways should remorse be induced in a bhikkhu who has been reproved in accordance with the Dhamma:
‘Venerable sir, you were reproved at the proper time, not at an improper time; this is sufficient for you to feel remorse.’”
The venerable one has been reproved with what is true, not with what is false; this is sufficient for you to feel remorse.
The venerable one has been reproved gently, not harshly; this is sufficient for you to feel remorse.
The venerable one has been reproved for the sake of benefit, not for the sake of harm; this is sufficient for you to feel remorse.
“Venerable sir, the Venerable was reproved with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner ill will;
it is sufficient for you to feel remorse. “Upāli, remorse should be induced in a monk who has been reproved according to the Dhamma by means of these five ways.
“Bhante, how many qualities should a monk who wishes to reprove another keep in mind within himself before reproving that other?”
“Upāli, a monk who wishes to reprove another should reprove him after attending to five qualities within himself:
compassion, the desire for his welfare, sympathy, the intent to emerge from the offense, and having the discipline as one’s primary concern.
Upāli, a monk who wishes to reprove another should reprove him after attending to these five qualities within himself.”
“But, Bhante, in how many qualities should a monk who has been reproved be established?
“Upāli, a monk who has been reproved should be established in two qualities:
in truth and in imperturbability.”
The second recitation section is finished.
This is the ninth chapter on the suspension of the Pātimokkha.
In this chapter, there are thirty cases.
Its summary verse:
On the Uposatha day, as far as it extended,
the wicked bhikkhu did not go out.
Expelled by Moggallāna—
what a marvel in the Conqueror’s dispensation!
And the gradual training, step by step.
The Saṅgha casts out the one who stands firm in his evil nature without overstepping [the bounds],
and they abandon even those who flow like rivers.
They all attain final Nibbāna,
for liberation has but a single flavor,
even though there are many teachings and disciplines.
The eight types of noble persons,
having used the ocean as a simile,
proclaimed the excellence within the Teaching.
On the uposatha day, no one knows our Pātimokkha;
they discard it only when it is too late.
One, two, three, four;
five, six, seven, eight,
and nine and ten.
Virtue, conduct, and view,
livelihood as the fourth part;
the pārājikas and the saṅghādisesas.
Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya,
Dukkaṭa— these comprise five categories,
as well as failure in virtue and conduct.
Regarding what has not been done and what has been done, according to the rule among the six parts:
the *pārājika* and the *saṅghādisesa*.
A grave offense, a *pācittiya*,
a *pāṭidesanīya*,
a *dukkaṭa*, and a *dubbhāsita*.
Failure in virtue and conduct,
failure in view and livelihood,
and what has been done or left undone in improper matters—
The holder of views regarding virtue and conduct— whether they have not been performed, have been performed,
or both performed and not performed;
Thus nine kinds have been stated according to reality as they are known:
the one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and the one whose act was unfinished.
Likewise, there is renunciation;
there is the approaching [of an offense], the taking back [of a formal act], and the discourse concerning that taking back.
Failure in virtue and conduct,
as well as failure in view;
what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
Know that in ten ways:
a bhikkhu sees a bhikkhu,
and another reports it to him.
He tells him exactly that,
and he suspends the Pātimokkha;
[the monk] emerges from the obstacle.
Kings, thieves, and water; humans and non-humans, as well as wild beasts and reptiles—
these are the dangers to the life of a brahmin.
By one of ten names,
or by one of those [names];
both legal and illegal.
Just as you know by means of the path:
"I shall obtain what is timely, beneficial, and connected to the goal; it will come to be."
Loving-kindness expressed through body and speech,
great learning, and both;
with one who is timely and gentle, [one should associate].
One should urge [another] with the aim of their welfare;
likewise, one should dispel [faults] through speech that is free from remorse.
For one who is spurred on by the goad of the Dhamma,
remorse is dispelled;
he is compassionate and sympathetic toward the welfare of others.
The practice for the one who reproves, aiming at rehabilitation,
has been proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One.
"Truthful and unshakable,
such is the nature of one who has been reproved.
The Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha is finished.
